This project is an exploration of linear models. Models are estimated by linear regression.  The data set is from Motor Trend magazine.

The assignment is based on estimation of 3 models:
1. mpg as a function of cyl
2. mpg as a function of disp
3  mpg as a function of both cyl and disp

Complete a linear model with data descripton, a model fit a, and a prediction of mpg based on weigth of 3050 lbs, with a displacement of 122 cubic inches (this is 2.5 L).

use an anova to compare model 2 with model 3

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE)
```
# Load the dataset (built-in)

```{r}
data(mtcars)
```


# View first 6 rows and summary
```{r}
head(mtcars)
```



# Model 1:

 mpg (miles per gallon) is the response (Y)
 wt (wt) is the predictor (X)

## data summary
### graphical summary
```{r}
plot(mpg ~ wt, data = mtcars, pch = 19)
```

This scatter plot shows that as weight (wt) increases, mpg decreases. The plot shows a strong negative relationship between weight and mpg.

### numerical summary
```{r}
cor(mtcars$mpg, mtcars$wt)
```
The correlation is -0.868, which shows a strong negative relationship between weight and mpg. As weight increases, mpg tends to decrease.
### model summary


```{r}
model1 <- lm(mpg ~ wt, data = mtcars)

summary(model1)
```


# Model 2:


 mpg (miles per gallon) is the response (Y)
 wt (wt) is the predictor (X)

## data summary

### graphical summary
```{r}
plot(mpg ~ disp, data = mtcars, pch = 19)
```

This scatter plot shows that as displacement (disp) increases, mpg decreases. The plot shows a strong negative relationship between displacement and mpg.

### numerical summary
```{r}
cor(mtcars$mpg, mtcars$disp)
```

### model summary


```{r}
model2 <- lm(mpg ~ disp, data = mtcars)
summary(model2)
```


# Model 3 :

 mpg (miles per gallon) is the response (Y)
 wt and disp are the predictors (X's)

## data summary
### graphical summary
```{r}
plot(mpg ~ wt+disp, data = mtcars)
```

This plot shows that as weight (wt) and displacement (disp) increase, mpg generally decreases. The plots show a strong negative relationship between the predictors and mpg.
### numerical summary
```{r}
cor(mtcars[, c("mpg", "wt", "disp")])
```
The numerical summary shows that mpg has a strong negative relationship with both weight (wt) and displacement (disp). Weight and displacement also have a strong positive relationship with each other.

### model summary

model3= lm(mpg ~ wt+disp, data = mtcars)
model summary (coefficients, R², etc.), summarize the fit

```{r}
model3= lm(mpg ~ wt+disp, data = mtcars)
summary(model3)
```
 mpg (miles per gallon) is the response (Y)
 wt (wt) and displacement (disp) are the predictors (X's)

## data summary

### graphical summary
```{r}
plot(mpg ~ wt+disp, data=mtcars)
```

The plots show that as weight (wt) and displacement (disp) increase, mpg generally decreases. Both plots show a strong negative relationship between the predictors and mpg.

### numerical summary
```{r}
cor(mtcars[, c("mpg", "wt", "disp")])
```

### model summary
```{r}
model3 <- lm(mpg ~ wt + disp, data = mtcars)
summary(model3)
```


# anova: compare models 2 and 3
```{r}
anova(model2, model3)
```


model3 <- lm(mpg ~ wt+disp, data = mtcars)

model summary (coefficients, R², etc.)

```{r}
summary(model3)
```

```{r}
anova_result <- anova(model1, model3)
print(anova_result)
```

# Discussion/Conclustions

Overall, weight (wt) appears to be the better predictor of mpg. Both weight and displacement have strong negative relationships with mpg, but when both predictors are included in Model 3, weight is statistically significant while displacement is not. The ANOVA comparisons also show that adding weight to the displacement model significantly improves the model, while adding displacement to the weight model does not significantly improve it. Therefore, Model 1 using weight alone is the preferred model because it is simpler and still explains a large amount of the variation in mpg.
